explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Luke says Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there (Luke 19:45). He didn't wait for a better time or send a polite note. He walked in and got to work.

Not quite, friend. The text says Jesus entered the temple courts and began to drive out those who were selling there (Luke 19:45). So He did find sellers, and He did start driving them out. I once got shoved to the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about being moved along, but this crowd had it coming.

You got it, baker. Jesus says, "It is written: 'My house will be a house of prayer.' But you have made it 'a den of robbers.'" (Luke 19:46). He starts with what God's house is meant to be. Then He says what the sellers made it instead.

Close on the sound of it, friend, but that's not the phrase. Jesus says the sellers have made it "a den of robbers." (Luke 19:46). He first quotes that the house will be "a house of prayer," so the contrast is right there in His words.
I see why you'd pick it, friend, but those aren't Jesus' words. He says, "But you have made it 'a den of robbers.'" (Luke 19:46). The thing He sets against the house of prayer is robbers, not idols.

Yes, baker. Luke says they could not find a way to kill Him, "because all the people hung on His words." (Luke 19:48). The leaders were intent on killing Him (Luke 19:47), but the crowd stuck close to every word Jesus said. Those leaders had the plan and still couldn't use it.

Not this time, friend. The text says the leaders were intent on killing Jesus, "Yet they could not find a way to do so, because all the people hung on His words." (Luke 19:47-48). So the statement is true as written. I'd say the crowd listening so closely is what stood in their way.

explanations.answer: By what authority He does these things
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They said, "Tell us, by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?" (Luke 20:2). It's a two-part question. They want to know the authority and who gave it.

explanations.answer: Why His disciples do not fast
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but that's a different question from a different day. Here the chief priests, scribes and elders ask, "by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?" (Luke 20:2). Fasting never comes up in this passage.

explanations.answer: How long He plans to stay in the city
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. Nobody asks about travel plans here. They ask, "by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?" (Luke 20:2). That's a much bigger question than how long He's staying.
Right, baker. Jesus asks, "John's baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?" (Luke 20:4). He answers their question with a question of His own. I'd say that gets everyone's attention in a hurry.
Good thinking, friend, but Moses doesn't come up here. Jesus asks, "John's baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?" (Luke 20:4). His question is about John, not about the law.
Not this one, friend. Jesus asks about John's baptism, not a throne. His words are, "John's baptism—was it from heaven, or from men?" (Luke 20:4). Nobody in this scene brings up David.

Yes, baker. The leaders say, "If we say, 'From heaven,' He will ask, 'Why did you not believe him?'" (Luke 20:5). They can already see the follow-up question coming. They're checking every answer before they give one.

Not quite, friend. The text says they reasoned, "If we say, 'From heaven,' He will ask, 'Why did you not believe him?'" (Luke 20:5). So that's exactly what they figured would happen. They saw that one coming from a mile away.

That's right, baker. The leaders say that if they answer "From men," all the people will stone them, "for they are convinced that John was a prophet." (Luke 20:6). The crowd had made up its mind about John. The leaders knew it.
Close, friend, but the people weren't convinced of that. The text says "they are convinced that John was a prophet." (Luke 20:6). The word is prophet.
Not this one, friend. The people are "convinced that John was a prophet." (Luke 20:6). Nobody in this passage calls John a king.

Yes, baker. The leaders say, "But if we say, 'From men,' all the people will stone us." (Luke 20:6). That's how serious they think the crowd's feelings about John are. I think that's why they get so careful with their words.
Good guess, friend, but that's not what they say. Their words are, "all the people will stone us." (Luke 20:6). That's a lot heavier than being shown the door.
I see the thinking, friend, but the leaders say something much sharper. They say, "all the people will stone us." (Luke 20:6). Tuning them out isn't what they're afraid of.

That's it, baker. Luke says, "So they answered that they did not know where it was from." (Luke 20:7). After all that huddling, that's what they came back with. I've given a few answers I'm not proud of myself, but that one is a doozy.
Close, friend, but that's not the word. The text says they answered "that they did not know where it was from." (Luke 20:7). It's know, not remember.
Not that one, friend. The leaders say they "did not know where it was from." (Luke 20:7). The text never says they stopped caring. It's the word know.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says the opposite: "Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things." (Luke 20:8). They wouldn't answer His question, so He doesn't answer theirs.

You got it, baker. After the leaders say they do not know, Jesus replies, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things." (Luke 20:8). He doesn't give them the answer they came for. The question they brought ends up back in their hands.
